e.t: This adjective refers to Abraham or describes someone as worthy of Abraham. It can identify a direct connection with Abraham, or praise a person by presenting that person as fitting Abraham’s honored character or example. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one sentence depends on whether it is naming Abraham himself or describing another person in relation to him.

This word means “love”: it describes giving affection, devotion, or deep regard toward someone or something. As a verb, it expresses the action of loving rather than simply naming love as a concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 246 times, including passages about loving God, people, and valued things. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains active love or devoted affection.

This noun means “hallowing”: the act of treating something as holy or setting it apart for sacred use. It names an action or process rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs seven times, appearing in Ezekiel, Amos, Sirach, and Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but its central idea remains hallowing or consecrating something as holy.

Adrazar, also rendered Athrazar, is a proper name for a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 11:14. The name itself identifies an individual; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s role in the account. This is a name preserved in the LXX text, so it should not be treated as a general theological or moral term.

Azaia, also rendered Azea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 11:4, identifying an individual. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the person’s specific role cannot be stated safely. The name itself functions as a proper name used to distinguish one person from others in the passage.

The word means “young goat,” referring to a juvenile member of the goat family. It is a noun, so it names an animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 10:3. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular role there. The word itself carries a straightforward animal reference.

This word describes someone or something that is following or attending on another. As an adjective, it identifies a person or thing characterized by accompanying, coming after, or serving alongside another. Its basic sense is straightforward and concerns a relationship of following rather than an independent action or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 4:17. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This noun refers to the foreskin, or describes someone as uncircumcised. It identifies the physical condition of having the foreskin rather than the circumcised state. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, beginning in Genesis and appearing mainly in passages concerned with circumcision or the distinction between circumcised and uncircumcised people. Its central meaning remains straightforward: the foreskin itself, or the condition of being uncircumcised, depending on how it functions in the sentence.

“Alimazonis” is a proper name, functioning as a personal or group designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears once, in 2 Chronicles 22:1. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a further descriptive meaning or enough surrounding verse text to explain whom it identifies. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the context of that passage.

This word means “remembrance”: the act or state of remembering someone or something. It is a noun that names remembrance itself rather than an action being commanded. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Psalms, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains keeping someone or something in mind.

This Greek LXX adverb means “opposite,” describing something located or positioned across from or contrary to something else. It functions as an adverb, so it modifies an action or description by indicating an opposing position or direction. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Song of Songs 6:5. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context.

This noun means “demonstration”—a clear showing or presentation that makes something evident. It refers to the act of setting something forth so that its truth, character, or force can be recognized. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 3 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being demonstrated in either passage.

This verb means “spit out”: to expel something from the mouth. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:18, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical contexts. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the basic meaning is the act of spitting something out.

This Greek LXX noun means “charioteer,” a person who drives or controls a chariot. It identifies someone by that occupation or role rather than describing a character quality or spiritual condition. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 9:4. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s specific role in that passage must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic meaning remains a chariot driver.

This noun refers to physical weakness or illness—“weakness; sickness.” It describes a condition in which a person lacks strength or is unwell. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, the word occurs 14 times, including passages translated with “sickness.” Its basic meaning remains broad enough to describe either the state of being weak or the condition of being sick; the surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent.

This word refers to an astrologer—a person associated with interpreting or observing the stars. It is a noun naming such a person, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Isaiah 47:13. The word’s basic meaning remains “astrologer”; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This LXX verb means “fasten from,” describing an action of fastening or attaching something in relation to a point or place. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing twice in Deuteronomy and twice in Proverbs. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains fastening. References include Deuteronomy 6:8, Deuteronomy 11:18, Proverbs 3:3, and Proverbs 6:21.

This Greek LXX verb means “purify; hallow”: it describes making something clean or setting it apart as sacred. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:13. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is the purification or consecration of something for a holy purpose.

Achias, also rendered Akhias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 11:29. Since the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding passage, its specific role there must be understood from that context. The name itself simply identifies a person.

Baithasimōth is a proper name, not an ordinary descriptive word with a translated meaning. It is identified by the related forms “Baithasimōth” and “Vethasimoth.” Since no further lexical definition is provided, the name should be retained rather than expanded into an inferred meaning. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Joshua 13:20. Its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage and cannot be determined from the name alone.

Bani, also rendered Vani, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name is associated with several listed individuals or groups in those genealogical and community records, but the available verse text does not establish one further meaning or identify a single person in every occurrence. Its precise referent therefore depends on the surrounding passage in each place.

This adjective means “better,” describing something as superior or preferable to another. It is used for comparisons involving people, choices, conditions, or outcomes, so its meaning depends on what is being compared. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 23 times, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and other books. The word therefore expresses improvement or advantage without by itself specifying whether the comparison concerns value, quality, position, or result.

Botanin, also rendered Votanin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or location in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once, in Joshua 13:26. Because it is a place name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it distinguishes one location from others. The name itself does not provide a further description of the place, and its precise significance depends on the surrounding passage.

“Fine linen” is a noun naming a refined textile or cloth. It refers to material rather than an action, person, or quality, and can identify the kind of fabric used for garments, furnishings, or other crafted items. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the word occurs 40 times, with most occurrences in Exodus and later uses extending through Ezekiel. Its precise significance in a particular passage depends on how that cloth is being used there.

This word means “owl,” referring to a nocturnal bird. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, appearing three times in its LXX corpus: twice in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy. Each occurrence appears within Israel’s dietary-law passages, where the owl is included among the birds being identified. The word itself names the bird; its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is found in Leviticus 11:16, Leviticus 11:19, and Deuteronomy 14:15.

This Greek LXX noun means “money-lending,” referring to the practice or activity of lending money. It names a financial arrangement rather than a person or an action directed toward a particular individual. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 18:33. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the business or practice of lending money. This term should therefore be understood as describing money-lending itself, not automatically as a judgment on every situation involving a loan.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something as “wretched” or “sorry”—in a pitiable, miserable, or regrettable condition. It functions as a descriptive word, pointing to a state that calls for pity or expresses distress over a condition. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Hosea, Nahum, and Baruch. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a description of misery or pitiable condition.

This Greek LXX word means “distinguishable”: something that can be recognized as different, clear, or set apart from other things. It functions as an adjective and may describe a person, thing, or feature that stands out sufficiently to be identified. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Genesis and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains recognizability or clear distinction.

This word means “tale,” referring to a narrated account or story. As a noun, it identifies something told or related, whether describing events, conveying instruction, or presenting a figurative account. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented in this corpus, showing that it can describe a spoken or written narrative across different kinds of biblical literature. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording and subject of the tale.

This verb means “dogmatize; follow decrees”: to establish an authoritative decree or to act according to one. It describes actions connected with binding decisions, commands, or official rules rather than a casual suggestion. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs six times, including passages in Esther, Daniel, and Maccabees. Its precise emphasis—making a decree or obeying one—depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the verb.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a maid or female servant and can also express the position of a subject or dependent person. Its central idea is a woman understood in relation to service or subordination, rather than a personal name or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 39 times, making it a recurring term for this kind of person or status.

This adjective describes someone or something as “puritanical” or “hard.” It can point to a strict, difficult, or unyielding quality, depending on the sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 30:2. The word’s basic sense identifies a challenging or rigid character rather than an action or object by itself. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This word means “shrine,” referring to a place set apart for worship or devotion. It is a noun, so it names a sacred site rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 1:2. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning identifies a shrine or worship site. It should be understood as a place associated with religious devotion, not as a general word for any building or location.

This noun means “peace”: a condition of calm, well-being, or harmony rather than conflict. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it can describe peaceful circumstances or the absence of hostility. The word occurs 262 times in the LXX corpus, showing that peace is a broad and recurring scriptural idea. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and whether the context concerns people, nations, or a person’s settled condition.

The word refers to a “siege engine”: a device used in attacking a fortified place. It is a noun naming military equipment rather than a person, action, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament’s deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees 13:43–44. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies equipment used in siege warfare, such as a machine brought against defensive walls.

The word means “business.” It is a noun referring to business as an activity or concern carried on by people or communities. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times in 11 verses, with occurrences ranging from Deuteronomy through Nahum. It appears most often in Ezekiel, but its central meaning remains business. The surrounding verse determines the particular matter or activity being discussed.

This noun refers to a “ransom” or a “propitiatory offering”—something given as payment for release or presented as an offering of propitiation. It names a thing, not an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice: once in 1 Samuel and once in Psalms. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use in either passage.

This verb means to laugh approvingly, expressing amusement or satisfaction toward something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 1:26. The word describes an approving or pleased laugh rather than simply any sound of laughter. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a favorable, almost mocking expression of enjoyment or satisfaction.

This verb means “confirm someone’s question” or, more simply, “confirm.” It describes an act of giving confirmation rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In Bible reading, it points to acknowledging or validating what someone has asked. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 7:9. The word’s basic action is clear, while its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something marked by reproach or shame. It can refer to a condition that brings disgrace, or to a person viewed as blameworthy or dishonored. Its central idea is not simply difficulty or weakness, but the shame attached to a person’s conduct or situation. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and 3 Maccabees, with four occurrences in Proverbs. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Esērsoual, also rendered Esirsual, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:28. Because no verse text or wider surrounding passage is provided here, the name itself does not establish further details about the person or the significance of the reference.

This adverb means “from inside” or “inwardly.” It describes something located within, coming out from within, or directed toward the inner side rather than the outside. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 24 times, often in descriptions of the inside of an object or structure. The precise force in a sentence depends on what inner place, direction, or source is being described.

This adjective describes something as “well-strung” or “vigorous”—strong, firm, and full of energy. It can describe a person or thing marked by active strength rather than weakness or slackness. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 12:23 and 4 Maccabees 7:10. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains an expression of firmness, strength, or vigor.

Ephratha, also rendered Efratha, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears as a named designation 17 times across 17 verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Micah. Its meaning is therefore primarily its identifying name, while the surrounding verse determines the particular person or place being identified. The supplied references show this name repeatedly associated with Old Testament locations and ancestral settings.

Zatholtha is a proper name, referring to an individual identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The name occurs once in the Greek text, at Esther 1:10. Its meaning is therefore the personal designation “Zatholtha”; what the named individual is doing or how the name functions in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Zoeleth is a proper name, preserved in English as “Zōeleth” or “Zoeleth.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. This Greek LXX word occurs once, in 1 Kings 1:9. Because no verse text or further lexical description is available here, the name itself supplies the clearest explanation: Zoeleth is a specific name whose exact referent must be understood from its surrounding passage.

This word is the proper name “Ēsau,” also rendered “Isav.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 106 times, most often in Genesis, with later appearances including Obadiah and 1 Maccabees. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Esau.

This verb means “sound”: to produce or give forth an audible noise. It can describe a sound becoming noticeable or spreading so that people hear it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, including descriptions of sounds connected with gatherings, movement, and public events. Its basic sense remains auditory rather than referring to silent thought or inward feeling. The surrounding verse determines what produces the sound and how forcefully it is heard.

This word means “basket,” referring to a container used to hold or carry something. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament and appears three times, all in Exodus 2:3, 2:5, and 2:6. These occurrences belong to the same account and use the word for the basket associated with the infant Moses. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: a physical basket or container, with the surrounding passage determining exactly how it is being used in each verse.

This adjective means “pleasing”—something that brings approval, delight, or satisfaction. It describes a person or thing favorably rather than naming an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Wisdom 3:14, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is pleasing there, but the word’s central idea is clear: favorable and welcome in someone’s sight.

This verb means “took them into exile,” describing the action of removing people from their homeland and bringing them into forced exile. It presents exile as an accomplished act carried out against others, rather than merely a condition of living away from home. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 8:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the removal of people into exile.

e.h: Private or for a Private Person
e.t: This adjective describes something belonging to a private person or relating to private rather than public life. It can function as a simple description of what is personal, individual, or not public. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is “for a private person; private,” and its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

“Properly sacred” describes something fitting for holy things or appropriate to what is sacred. As an adjective, the word identifies a person, action, or quality as having a genuinely sacred character. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains what is rightly or fittingly sacred.

This word is a proper personal name, rendered “Iephonnē” or “Iefonni.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, it appears 17 times, beginning in Numbers and continuing through Joshua, 1 Chronicles, Deuteronomy, and Sirach. The name’s precise identification and significance depend on the passage in which it appears; the word itself functions simply as a personal designation.

This is a personal name, rendered “Iōsedek” or “Iosethek.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, the name occurs 13 times, with occurrences in Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, and Sirach. Its precise identification in any particular passage depends on the surrounding text, but the word itself functions as a proper name. It remains a Greek LXX name and should not be treated as a general title or translated concept.

This verb means “close”—to shut something or bring it into a closed position. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used four times, all in four Old Testament verses: three in Isaiah and one in Lamentations. Its basic sense remains an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The surrounding wording determines what is being closed in each passage, but the word itself consistently points to the act of closing. It appears in Isaiah 6:10, Isaiah 29:10, Isaiah 33:15, and Lamentations 3:45.

This adjective describes something that is “in the mind”—present in a person’s thoughts or inner consideration. It points to what someone has mentally in view, rather than naming an outward action or object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Isaiah and once in Micah, so its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence. Its central meaning remains the inward mental presence or consideration of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut in pieces.” It describes the action of dividing or chopping something into separate pieces, rather than merely moving or distributing it. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including five Old Testament occurrences and one in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains physical cutting into pieces.

This LXX verb means “crouch down” or “lie crouching.” It describes lowering oneself and remaining close to the ground in a crouched position. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, including passages in Joshua, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says about the person or creature being described, but its central idea remains a lowered, crouching posture.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “straighten out” or “direct.” It describes making something straight or guiding it toward a chosen course. As an action word, it can refer to setting a path in order or directing movement, conduct, or purpose. The word occurs 52 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, so its basic idea is used broadly rather than being limited to one kind of situation. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being straightened or directed there.

This verb means “ridicule”: to make someone an object of scorn or contempt. It describes an action directed toward a person rather than a thing, expressing derision through words or conduct. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 5:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the act of ridiculing someone.

This word means “judgment”: a decision, ruling, or determination concerning what is right or deserved. As a noun, it can refer to the judgment itself rather than the act of judging. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it is used 218 times, showing a broad and established use for decisions or judgments. It appears in passages connected with laws, instructions, and claims about justice, but its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun refers to “talk” or “prattle”—spoken words viewed as speech or chatter. Its basic sense is broad and does not by itself identify whether the speech is wise, serious, or foolish; the surrounding passage determines that. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in 1 Kings and Ezekiel. It appears in passages involving speech directed toward or about people, but the word itself simply names talk or prattle rather than describing a particular message or attitude.

This word means a washing tub or basin—a container used for washing. It is a noun referring to a physical vessel, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle and temple furnishings. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, all in Old Testament verses, from Exodus through 2 Chronicles. The word’s basic sense remains focused on the container itself rather than the act of washing. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object or ritual being described.

This is a proper name rendered “Magedō” or “Mayetho.” It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Judges 1:27 and once in Isaiah 10:28. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific reference cannot be explained further here, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Magedō or Mayetho.

This verb means “soothsay”: to engage in or perform soothsaying. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twelve times, all within Old Testament verses, so its use belongs to that corpus and not to the Greek New Testament. It appears in passages from Deuteronomy through Micah, with seven occurrences in Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Mellēthi” or “Mellithi,” rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 25:26. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough verse text to explain more about its bearer or significance. Its precise reference is therefore best understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “lengthen”—to make something extend farther or become longer. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in Isaiah and twice in Ezekiel. Its references are Isaiah 44:14, Ezekiel 12:25, and Ezekiel 12:28. Without the surrounding verse text, the precise object being lengthened cannot be stated here, but the central idea remains extension in size, duration, or reach. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what the verb acts upon.

This Greek LXX verb means “hire” or “let out for hire.” It describes the act of engaging someone for work or making something available in return for payment. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 24:12; the surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which the action appears.

“Scarcely” is an adverb that marks something as happening only to a very small degree or as barely occurring. It narrows a statement, showing that what is described is close to not happening at all. This LXX word appears eight times across the corpus, in Proverbs, Wisdom, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. It modifies the action or statement being described rather than naming a person or object. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Mouchaios, also rendered Mukheos, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament text of Esther, it appears twice, in Esther 1:16 and Esther 1:21. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its role in identifying a person, while the surrounding passage supplies the details about that person. The name itself does not provide a broader spiritual or conceptual definition.

This word means “bar,” referring to a firm piece used to support, join, secure, or block something. In the Greek LXX, it commonly describes structural bars used with the tabernacle and other objects, and it can also refer to a bar that closes or fastens an entrance. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 39 times in the LXX corpus, with many uses connected to construction, equipment, or security.

This word means “ephah,” the name of a biblical measure used in the Old Testament. It refers to a defined quantity, especially in passages involving grain or other offerings, though its precise amount is not given here. As a noun, it identifies the measure itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times, from Leviticus through Ezekiel, showing its use in Israel’s worship and law-related measurements.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a “drill sergeant” or an “armed fighter”—a person connected with military training or fighting with weapons. It names a person rather than an action or object. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Isaiah 13 (Isaiah 13:4 and 13:5). Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is a person involved in preparing for or carrying out armed combat.

This adjective means “of all sorts,” describing something that includes different kinds or varieties. It broadens the noun or idea it modifies rather than naming one particular kind. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here: once in Daniel and four times in the Deuterocanonical books. Its basic sense remains consistent across these occurrences, while the exact force in any verse depends on the noun and surrounding sentence. It is therefore a general word for variety, range, or differing kinds.

This Greek LXX noun means “walking about” or “walking,” referring to movement from place to place. It names the act or manner of walking rather than expressing a command to walk. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, including uses in Job, Proverbs, and Ezekiel, and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This word means “of a mollusk,” referring to something connected with a shellfish or other soft-bodied aquatic creature. It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament corpus, though its precise reference in Esther 1:6 depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not available here. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, specifically at Esther 1:6, and its meaning remains focused on association with a mollusk rather than expressing an action or personal quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “superfluity,” referring to more than is needed or appropriate. It describes an excess rather than something merely present in an ordinary amount. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 31:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to an amount that goes beyond what is necessary or expected.

This noun means “profit,” referring to gain or benefit obtained from something. It describes what a person receives as an advantage or return. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in the Wisdom of Solomon: once in Wisdom 13:19 and once in Wisdom 14:2. The surrounding wording determines whether the profit is material or concerns some other benefit, but the central idea remains gain or advantage.

This noun refers to a crop. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Leviticus 1:16. Its basic meaning is straightforward: it identifies a crop rather than describing an action, person, or quality. It functions as a naming word for that kind of thing, not as a verb or descriptive adjective. The exact significance of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This verb means “overthrow” or “overturn”: to cause something established to fall, be reversed, or be brought down. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:23. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is decisive reversal or collapse of what had been standing or established.

This verb means to “honour”: to treat someone as worthy of respect, recognition, or special regard. It describes an action directed toward a person rather than merely an inner feeling. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in two different deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains the active expression of honour toward someone, while the surrounding sentence determines whether that honour is shown through words, conduct, or public regard.

Ribai, also rendered Rhive, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:31. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes the person’s designation but does not provide further meaning about his character, role, or significance. Its precise reference is therefore understood from the passage in which the name appears.

Salamiel is a proper name for a person, also rendered “Salamil.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs seven times, all in Numbers, from Numbers 1:6 through Numbers 34:20. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and explain his particular role in each passage.

This is a proper name, rendered “Saunis” or “Savnis,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 46:16, so its ordinary lexical role is simply to identify a person in the biblical record. The available information does not provide an additional definition or explain the name’s meaning.

Setri is a personal name, identifying a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament and does not carry an additional definition beyond the name itself. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Exodus 6:22. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and family record, but its basic lexical function is simply to identify the person named Setri.

This Greek word means “strength” or “might,” referring to power or force. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings to name strength rather than describe an action. The word occurs four times in this Greek corpus: three times in Job and once in 3 Maccabees. Its repeated rendering as “strength” supports the central sense, while the gloss “might” shows that it can also express power or capability. The surrounding verse determines how that strength is being discussed.

This Greek LXX verb means “scope out” or “look out for”: it describes actively watching for something or paying careful attention to it. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on attentive observation and watchfulness.

Souphir, also rendered Sufir, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures. The word identifies a named person, place, or other designated entity, but the available information does not specify which kind here. It occurs five times in the LXX corpus: four times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the wording of each passage.

This noun means “campaign” or “war,” referring to organized military action or a period of armed conflict. It names the undertaking itself rather than a person who fights or a specific weapon. In this Greek biblical corpus, the word appears once, at 4 Maccabees 9:24. The surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there, but its basic meaning remains a military campaign or war.

This Greek LXX verb means “with,” expressing being together with or accompanying someone. It describes presence alongside another person rather than an action performed alone. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages in Joshua, Chronicles, Job, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any sentence depends on who is present with whom, but its central idea is companionship, shared presence, or association.

This verb means to go forth together—to leave or proceed in company with others. It describes shared movement rather than simply going alone. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Judges 13:25. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the joint action of setting out or moving onward together.

Sosan is a proper name, referring to a person named Sosan in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but as an individual’s name. Within the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in three verses of 1 Chronicles 2. The available rendering preserves the name as “Sosan,” so no broader ordinary meaning is established for it apart from its use as a personal name.

This Greek LXX verb means “give birth” or “produce.” It describes bringing forth a child and can also refer more broadly to producing something. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. It occurs 232 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being brought forth and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “three,” the number that identifies a group of three people, objects, or units, or describes something occurring in a set of three. It can function as a number word and may qualify a noun or stand in for the counted group. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 331 times, showing regular use wherever Scripture counts or measures. Its basic meaning remains numerical; the surrounding verse determines what three items or persons are being identified.

This adjective means “round,” describing a shape or form that is circular rather than straight or angular. It appears three times in the LXX, all in Proverbs, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word functions as a descriptive term, identifying the shape or quality of something being discussed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “cheese,” naming the food itself. In the Greek Old Testament and its deuterocanonical books, it appears 30 times across 29 verses. Its use spans historical, poetic, prophetic, and later Jewish writings, so it functions as an ordinary concrete noun rather than a title or abstract idea. The word occurs from 2 Samuel through 2 Maccabees, including references in 2 Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Psalms.

This noun means “lintel,” the beam or stone placed across the top of a doorway or other opening. It names a structural part of a building rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 6:4. Its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself refers to the architectural feature above the opening.

Phalaris is a proper name, referring to a person named Phalaris. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees.5.20 and 3 Maccabees.5.42. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun, its basic meaning is the individual it identifies, not an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what is said about Phalaris in either passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to thought or care—the inward attention given to something or someone. It can describe concern that occupies the mind, whether expressed as care for another or as serious thought about a matter. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Job, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is thoughtful concern or care.

This Greek LXX verb describes land becoming dry or lying waste. It can refer either to the condition of dry ground or to land being left desolate. The basic idea is loss of fertility or habitation, expressed as a change in the land’s state rather than as an action involving a person. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Nahum.

Chobor, also rendered Khovor, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 46:17. The supplied lexical meaning identifies the name itself, but the available information does not specify whether it names a person, place, or other entity. Its precise referent therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name referring to Oronaim, also represented as Ōrōnaim or Oronem. It is not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily identification of a named place or location. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Jeremiah 31:3, 31:5, and 31:34. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what is associated with Oronaim in each occurrence.
